text:
Card games and social gatherings don’t tell you everything, but asking someone out of the blue, “What did you do wrong in your past relationships?” would make for a pretty weird date.

At the right time, though, in the right way (especially if they bring it up tangentially), I would ask about their past relationships, especially the recent ones. If every story ends with everything being the other person’s fault, I’d ask, “Okay, so what lessons did you find for yourself?”

“I have baggage” isn't as useful as learning what you're having trouble with now. What might make it hard for you to function well in a relationship?

I’d want both of us to be honest about how effective we actually are at handling our own issues. What addictions or impulsive behaviors can’t we reliably control? What are we probably going to ask forgiveness for more than once? That tells me more than either of us proclaiming that we’re healed.

Look at the most recent conflicts and ask if you were able to regulate yourself during them. What did you do to the other person, and how did you repair the damage afterward? Not doing can be just as bad as overdoing. If conflict makes you shut down, does it mean you stop talking to your partner for days, leaving them feeling abandoned?

Has your judgment gotten better, or would your friends or exes say you keep falling for the same stuff?
reader: someone dating who wants to learn how a new partner handles their flaws and conflicts, without interrogating them on a date

sentences.s: Card games and social gatherings don’t tell you everything, but asking someone out of the blue, “What did you do wrong in your past relationships?” would make for a pretty weird date.
sentences.payoff: the reader learns that the games and gatherings they have been using won't show them everything, and that the obvious fix, asking straight out about past mistakes on a date, is the wrong one, so they look for the better way the next paragraph gives
sentences.follows: it turns from the section before, on card games and social gatherings as ways to get to know someone, to what those can't show: how someone handles their own flaws

sentences.s: At the right time, though, in the right way (especially if they bring it up tangentially), I would ask about their past relationships, especially the recent ones.
sentences.payoff: the reader learns when and how to raise past relationships instead: at the right moment, gently, best when the other person brings it up, and about the recent ones
sentences.follows: it answers the sentence before: if the blunt question is wrong, here is the way to ask

sentences.s: If every story ends with everything being the other person’s fault, I’d ask, “Okay, so what lessons did you find for yourself?”
sentences.payoff: the reader gets the warning sign to listen for, every story blaming the other person, and the one question that tests it
sentences.follows: it says what to listen for once they are talking about past relationships
sentences.link: If every story ends with everything being the other person’s fault

sentences.s: “I have baggage” isn't as useful as learning what you're having trouble with now.
sentences.payoff: the reader learns that a vague admission tells them little, and that what someone struggles with now is what to find out
sentences.follows: after the question about lessons learned, it turns to the answer people often give instead, "I have baggage"

sentences.s: What might make it hard for you to function well in a relationship?
sentences.payoff: the reader gets the concrete question to ask in place of "I have baggage"
sentences.follows: it is the question the sentence before says is more useful
sentences.link: What might make it hard for you

sentences.s: I’d want both of us to be honest about how effective we actually are at handling our own issues.
sentences.payoff: the reader learns that the honesty goes both ways, and that it is about how well each of you actually handles your issues
sentences.follows: it widens the questions from the other person to both of us

sentences.s: What addictions or impulsive behaviors can’t we reliably control?
sentences.payoff: the reader gets the first concrete thing to be honest about: what neither of you can reliably control
sentences.follows: it says what "handling our own issues" means in practice

sentences.s: What are we probably going to ask forgiveness for more than once?
sentences.payoff: the reader gets the second: the mistakes each of you will likely repeat and need forgiving for
sentences.follows: it continues the honest inventory from what we can't control to what we will repeat
sentences.link: What are we probably going to ask forgiveness for

sentences.s: That tells me more than either of us proclaiming that we’re healed.
sentences.payoff: the reader learns why this inventory beats someone saying they're healed
sentences.follows: it closes the inventory by saying what it is worth compared with the usual claim

sentences.s: Look at the most recent conflicts and ask if you were able to regulate yourself during them.
sentences.payoff: the reader learns where to look to see how someone really handles trouble: their most recent conflicts, starting with whether they could regulate themselves
sentences.follows: after the honest inventory, it gives the evidence to check it against: what actually happened in recent conflicts
sentences.link: Look at the most recent conflicts

sentences.s: What did you do to the other person, and how did you repair the damage afterward?
sentences.payoff: the reader gets the next two things to look for in those conflicts: the harm done and the repair
sentences.follows: it continues the look at the recent conflicts from how they felt to what they did
sentences.link: What did you do to the other person

sentences.s: Not doing can be just as bad as overdoing.
sentences.payoff: they see that holding back in a conflict, shutting down instead of lashing out, harms a partner too, which is why the next question asks about it
sentences.follows: after the harm and the repair, it turns to the other way a conflict goes wrong, the one people don't count as harm
sentences.link: Not doing can be just as bad

sentences.s: If conflict makes you shut down, does it mean you stop talking to your partner for days, leaving them feeling abandoned?
sentences.payoff: they get the concrete check for shutting down: whether it meant days of silence that left the partner feeling abandoned
sentences.follows: it is the case the sentence before names, asked of their own record
sentences.link: If conflict makes you shut down

sentences.s: Has your judgment gotten better, or would your friends or exes say you keep falling for the same stuff?
sentences.payoff: they get the last test, over time: whether they learn from conflicts, judged also by the people who saw them
sentences.follows: after what happened in the recent conflicts, it asks what came of them over time, so it closes the section

placement: The opener follows the card-games section it turns from; the section then goes: when to ask about past relationships, what to ask instead of "I have baggage", the honesty both people owe, what to look at in recent conflicts (the harm, the repair, the shutting down), and last the long view, whether judgment gets better, as its own paragraph. His fix of 2026-11-23 put the shut-down question next to the harm and repair it belongs with.

same_point: "ask forgiveness for more than once" and "keep falling for the same stuff" both touch repeated mistakes, the one about what's to come, the other about the record; no other paragraph makes the opener's point or the shut-down one.

questions.Q1: PASS: each paragraph opens on its point: the first on what games can't show, the fifth on where to look, the last on "if you tell me you shut down"
questions.Q2: N/A: no instructions to a helper; these are questions the reader asks a partner or themselves
questions.Q3: PASS: "the most recent conflicts", "stopped talking to your partner for days", "addictions or impulsive behaviors" say which thing exactly
questions.Q4: PASS: no term a high-school graduate wouldn't know; "regulate yourself" is plain in a section about conflicts
questions.Q5: PASS: the first paragraph's "but" turns from what games can't show to why the blunt question is wrong; "though" answers it with the right time; the last "And" adds one answer to the questions before it
questions.Q6: PASS: the order follows the reader: what games can't show, when to ask, what to ask, what to look for, one follow-up
questions.Q7: PASS: every line is about the reader's own case, a new partner's flaws and conflicts while dating
questions.Q9: PASS: one question to a sentence; the last sentence's two parts are one follow-up (what shutting down meant, and what it did to the partner)

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
